rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad considers it very probable that this exhortation first addressed Muhammad, as most classical commentators say.
rows.anchor: it is very probable that - as most of the classical commentators point out - this exhortation was in the first instance addressed to the Prophet Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exhortation also applies to every person who reads the Qur'an, at any time.
rows.anchor: there is no doubt that it applies to every person, at all times, who reads the Qur'an.

words: مِن قَبْلِ أَن يُقْضَىٰٓ إِلَيْكَ وَحْيُهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Qur'an is one coordinated whole, readers should let its full message shape their understanding and avoid conclusions from isolated verses; Asad links this to 25:32 and 75:16-19.
rows.anchor: all its component parts - phrases, sentences, verses and surahs - form one integral, coordinated whole

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam forgot God's command and lacked firmness of purpose.
rows.anchor: but he forgot it, and We found no firmness of purpose in him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commandment, more precisely a warning, is stated in 20:117.
rows.anchor: The relevant divine commandment - or, rather, warning - is spelled out in verse 117.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage connects to 20:99, which introduces earlier stories, and uses Adam to illustrate a recurring human neglect of spiritual truths.
rows.anchor: The present passage connects with the statement in verse 99

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the story as showing that neglect of spiritual truths recurs throughout human history, with Adam symbolizing humanity as elsewhere in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: negligence of spiritual truths is one of the recurrent characteristics of the human race (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels prostrated themselves before Adam, while Iblis refused.
rows.anchor: they all prostrated themselves, save Iblis, who refused [to do it]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God warns Adam and his wife that their foe could drive them from the garden and make Adam unhappy.
rows.anchor: Verily, this is a foe unto thee and thy wife: so let him not drive the two of you out of this garden and render thee unhappy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the garden Adam is provided against hunger, nakedness, thirst, and exposure to the sun.
rows.anchor: Behold, it is provided for thee that thou shalt not hunger here or feel naked,[105]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes the wording literally as “so that thou wilt become unhappy” and refers readers to his note on the garden in surah 2.
rows.anchor: Lit., "so that thou wilt become unhappy". Regarding the significance of "the garden" spoken of here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the phrase literally says “be naked,” Asad argues it means that innocent humans originally felt no nakedness without clothes; he cites 20:121 and 7:22, and points to the allegory in 7:20.
rows.anchor: only after their fall from grace did Adam and Eve become "conscious of their nakedness"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God chose Adam for grace, accepted his repentance, and gave him guidance.
rows.anchor: and accepted his repentance, and bestowed His guidance upon him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the descent from innocence and the onset of mutual enmity, whoever follows God's guidance will neither stray nor be unhappy.
rows.anchor: there shall most certainly come unto you guidance from Me: and he who follows My guidance will not go astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning away from remembrance brings a narrow life and blindness on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: his shall be a life of narrow scope; [109] and on the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrow life is sterile and spiritually constricted, lacking real meaning or purpose, and it becomes a source of hereafter suffering.
rows.anchor: sterile and spiritually narrow, without any real meaning or purpose: and this, as is indicated in the subsequent clause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad cross-references his rendering of man asrafa to his discussion of musrif, a participial noun from the same root, in surah 10.
rows.anchor: Regarding this rendering of the phrase man asrafa, see surah 10, note 21

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Resurrection Day the sinner asks why he is blind despite having had sight; God answers that he ignored the divine messages and is now forgotten.
rows.anchor: O my Sustainer! Why hast Thou raised me up blind, whereas [on earth]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God recompenses those who waste themselves and disbelieve in His messages with punishment in the life to come that is severe and enduring.
rows.anchor: and does not believe in his Sustainer's messages: and, indeed, the suffering

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth-deniers demand a miracle from Muhammad, although clear evidence of the divine writ is already found in earlier scriptures.
rows.anchor: would but produce for us a miracle from his Sustainer! [119] [But] has there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demanded sign would prove Muhammad's prophetic mission; deniers often make belief in the Qur'an conditional on tangible miracles, as in 6:109.
rows.anchor: in proof of his prophetic mission: cf. 6:109 and, many other instances in which the deniers of the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question asks whether the Qur'an conveys the same fundamental truths as earlier prophetic revelations.
rows.anchor: Does not the Qur'an express the same fundamental truths as were expressed in the revelations granted to the earlier prophets?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad also sees an allusion to earlier predictions of Muhammad, including Deuteronomy 18:15, 18 and Jesus' Comforter sayings; he discusses these at 2:42 and 61:6.
rows.anchor: the above rhetorical question contains an allusion to the predictions of the advent of Muhammad to be found in the earlier scriptures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All are waiting for the future; the Judgment will reveal who followed the even path and who found guidance.
rows.anchor: waiting [for what the future may bring]: [122] wait, then, [for the Day of Judgment - ]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone, whatever their beliefs or circumstances, hopes that their chosen way of life will prove right.
rows.anchor: no man, whatever his persuasion or condition, can ever cease to hope that the way of life chosen by him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God set firm mountains to keep the earth from swaying and laid broad paths so people can find their way.
rows.anchor: (31} And [are they not aware that] We have set up firm mountains on earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky is a well-secured canopy, yet people turn away from its signs.
rows.anchor: and [that] We have set up the sky as a canopy well-secured?[41] And yet, they stubbornly turn away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created night, day, sun, and moon, all of which float through space.
rows.anchor: and [fail to see that] it is He who has created the night and th e day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the protected-sky phrase seems to have a similar meaning to the first sentence of 13:2.
rows.anchor: See note 4 on the first sentence of 13:2, which seems to have a similar meaning.

words: مَا لَا يَنفَعُكُمْ شَيْـًۭٔا وَلَا يَضُرُّكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham argues that idols are unworthy of worship because they can neither benefit nor harm, and urges his people to reason.
rows.anchor: Do you then worship, instead of God, something that cannot benefit you in any way, nor harm you?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In anger Jonah assumes God has no power over him, then cries out in distress, affirming God's oneness and glory and confessing his wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: when he went off in wrath, thinking that We had no power over him![83] But then he cried out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “great fish” refers to Jonah, whose swallowing by a great fish is also mentioned at 37:139 onward and narrated in the Book of Jonah.
rows.anchor: the Prophet Jonah, who is said to have been swallowed by a "great fish", as mentioned in 37:139 ff.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says Jonah was sent to Nineveh; after his preaching was ignored, he angrily abandoned his mission, which 37:140 likens to a runaway slave's flight.
rows.anchor: Jonah was a prophet sent to the people of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. At first his preaching was disregarded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah's temporary punishment and later rescue and redemption form an allegory; this and the next verse allude to his punishment, repentance, and salvation, also told in 37:139-148.
rows.anchor: The allegory of his temporary punishment and his subsequent rescue and redemption is referred to elsewhere in the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The redemption of Jonah's people is separately mentioned in 10:98 and 37:147-148.
rows.anchor: The redemption of Jonah's people is mentioned in 10:98 and 37:147-148.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final confession literally says, “I was among the wrongdoers.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "I was among the wrongdoers".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God had declared in books of divine wisdom that His righteous servants would inherit the earth.
rows.anchor: We laid it down in all the books of divine wisdom that My righteous servants shall inherit the earth

words: إِنَّ فِى هَٰذَا لَبَلَٰغًۭا لِّقَوْمٍ عَٰبِدِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This message is for people who truly worship God.
rows.anchor: herein, behold, there is a message for people who [truly] worship God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr literally means “the reminder”; Asad points to 21:10 for its deeper Qur'anic implications.
rows.anchor: Lit., "after the reminder (adh-dhikr)". For the deeper implications of the Qur'anic term dhikr

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari treats zabur, literally scripture or book, as a generic term for any book of wisdom and thus for every divine scripture revealed to prophets.
rows.anchor: any and all of the divine scriptures revealed by God to the prophets [Tabari]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that the righteous inherit the earth echoes 3:139: faith and righteous conduct let humanity reach the heights intended by the Creator's grace.
rows.anchor: is obviously an echo of the promise, "You are bound to rise high if you are (truly] believers"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pilgrims are to end their self-denial, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient Temple.
rows.anchor: let them bring to an end their state of self-denial, [42] and let them fulfil the vows

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honouring God's sacred commands benefits the worshipper; cattle are lawful except what God specifies as forbidden.
rows.anchor: if one honours God's sacred commandments, it will redound to his own good in his Sustainer's sight.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage commands avoidance of idolatrous practices and every untrue word, and likens associating divinity with anything beside God to a catastrophic fall.
rows.anchor: Shun, then, [all that God has forbidden and, most of all,] the loathsome evil of idolatrous beliefs and practices; [45]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's principle is that anything not explicitly forbidden is lawful in itself; Asad refers to 5:3.
rows.anchor: Once again, the Qur'an stresses the principle that everything that has not been explicitly forbidden is per se lawful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awthan means concrete idols, but broadly also covers false beliefs, practices, and values treated as objects of worship; this wider sense leads into the ban on untrue speech.
rows.anchor: denotes not merely actual, concrete images of false deities but also, in its widest sense, everything that is associated with false beliefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers attain a happy state through humility in prayer and active pursuit of inner purity.
rows.anchor: TRULY, to a happy state shall attain the believe rs: (23:2) those who humble themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successful turn from frivolity and guard chastity within marriage; those who seek to exceed that boundary transgress.
rows.anchor: and who turn away from all that is frivolous, (23:4) and who are intent on inner purity;[1]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successful keep trusts and pledges and guard their prayers from worldly intent.
rows.anchor: and who guard their prayers [from all worldly intent].

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zakah here means working for or actively promoting inner purity, an interpretation also advanced by Abu Muslim.
rows.anchor: which is the meaning of zakah in this context (Zamakhshari; the same interpretation has been advanced by Abu Muslim)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarn literally means a generation; Asad refers to 6:5 for the term's wider sense.
rows.anchor: Lit., "a generation (qarn) of others". For a wider meaning of the term qarn. see surah 6, note 5.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After earlier peoples, God raised new generations and sent each a messenger from among them to call them to worship Him alone and be conscious of Him.
rows.anchor: AND AFTER those [people of old] We gave rise to new generations; (23:32)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people's elite reject truth and the afterlife amid worldly ease and plenty, which has corrupted them.
rows.anchor: the great ones among his peopl e, who refused to acknowledge the truth and gave the lie

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They dismiss the messenger as an ordinary human and reject his promise that people will be raised after becoming dust and bones.
rows.anchor: nothing but a mortal like yourselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers assert that earthly life is all there is, deny resurrection, and accuse the messenger of inventing lies about God.
rows.anchor: There is no life beyond our life in this world: we die and we live [but once], and we shall never be raised

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari explains the phrase as saying that God granted them ease and plenty in worldly life; Asad points to his fuller discussion of tarifa at 11:116.
rows.anchor: Thus Tabari interprets the concise but meaningful phrase atrafnahum fi 'l-hayati 'd-dunya.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophet asks God for help against his people's accusation of lying, and God says they will soon regret it.
rows.anchor: Succour me against their accusation of lying!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A just and unavoidable blast overtakes the evildoers, leaving them like flotsam and scum on a torrent.
rows.anchor: And then the blast [of Our punishment) overtook them, justly and unavoidably,[20] and We caused them

rows.speaker: Righib
rows.claim: Righib says bi'l-haqq here combines justice, wisdom, reality, inescapability, and suitability to the case, so any translation is approximate.
rows.anchor: combines in this instance the concepts of justice, wisdom, reality, inescapability, and consonance with the exigencies of the case under consideration (Righib)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If truth followed human likes and dislikes, the cosmos and all life would collapse; the divine writ brings their reminder, yet they turn away.
rows.anchor: But if the truth [41] were in accord with their own likes a nd dislikes, the heavens

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here al-haqq means the reality of all creation.
rows.anchor: the reality of all creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the universe, especially human life, were as meaningless and purposeless as deniers imagine, nothing could endure and all would have perished in chaos.
rows.anchor: if the universe - and, especially, human life had been as devoid of meaning and purpose as they imagine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders dhikr as “reminder” here and refers to 21:10 for the term's meaning.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of the term dhikr; see note 13 on 21:10.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet seeks no worldly payment from them; God's recompense is better because He is the best provider.
rows.anchor: Or dost thou [O Muhammad] ask of them any worldly recompense? But [they ought to know that]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kharj and kharaj are broadly synonymous, both meaning recompense.
rows.anchor: The terms kharj and kharaj which occur in the above verse are more or less synonymous, both of them denoting "recompense".

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari sees kharj as slightly narrower than kharaj; Asad's translation marks the first as worldly recompense and leaves God's recompense unrestricted to this world or the hereafter.
rows.anchor: According to Zamakhshari, however, there is a slight difference between these two expressions, kharj being more restricted in its meaning than kharaj

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad calls people to a straight way, but those who deny the afterlife deviate from it.
rows.anchor: And, verily, thou callest them onto a straight way - (23:74) but, behold, those who will not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if God showed mercy and removed distress, they would persist arrogantly, stumbling blindly.
rows.anchor: And even were We to show them mercy and remove whatever distress might befall them [in this life], [45]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God asks the condemned whether His messages had been conveyed to them and whether they habitually denied them.
rows.anchor: Were not My messages conveyed unto you, and were you [not] wont to give them the lie?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned blame their misfortune for leading them astray and beg to leave their suffering, promising to be counted among evildoers if they sin again.
rows.anchor: O our Sustainer! Our bad luck has overwhelmed us, and so we went astray![62]
